Page 1
Medical Health Knowledge Base
Enriched PDF knowledge source for learning and building a Retrieval-Augmented Generation
(RAG) chatbot
Purpose: This document is intentionally rich in headings, paragraphs, FAQs, tables, terminology, examples,
and repeated concepts so it can be used to practice PDF ingestion, parsing, chunking, embeddings, vector
search, retrieval, metadata, prompting, and RAG evaluation.

metadata, prompting, and RAG evaluation.
Important: This is an educational synthetic knowledge base created for software/RAG practice. It is not
medical advice, a diagnostic reference, or a substitute for a qualified healthcare professional.
Suggested project: Build a chatbot that answers questions only from retrieved passages in this document,
clearly states when the document does not contain enough information, and encourages professional medical
care for urgent or personal medical decisions.

Page 3
1. How to Use This Document for RAG
A knowledge source for RAG is more useful when it contains enough variety to create meaningful retrieval
problems. This document includes short definitions, longer explanations, tables, FAQs, and related concepts
expressed in different wording. For example, a user may ask about “high blood sugar,” while a passage may
use the term “hyperglycemia.” A good embedding and retrieval system should recognize that these concepts
can be related.

recognize that these concepts
can be related.
For ingestion practice, extract text page by page and preserve metadata such as document name, page
number, section heading, and chunk index. During chunking, experiment with fixed-size chunks,
sentence-aware chunks, paragraph-aware chunks, and recursive splitting. Do not assume that one chunking
strategy is universally correct.
For retrieval practice, ask questions that use synonyms, paraphrases, broad concepts, and specific details.

broad concepts, and specific details.
Compare the retrieved chunks with the expected evidence. Record whether the correct passage appears in
top-1, top-3, or top-5 results.
For generation practice, instruct the model to answer only from retrieved context. If the context is insufficient,
the chatbot should say that the available knowledge base does not contain enough information rather than
inventing an answer.

Page 4

both everyday language and technical terms. The following glossary is intentionally compact so individual

Page 5
3. Preventive Health and Lifestyle
Preventive health focuses on reducing avoidable risks, detecting selected conditions early, and maintaining
behaviors that support general health. Prevention recommendations vary according to age, personal history,
family history, medications, pregnancy status, and other factors.
Nutrition is one part of preventive health.

Nutrition is one part of preventive health. A balanced eating pattern generally emphasizes a variety of
vegetables and fruits, whole grains or other high-fiber foods, appropriate protein sources, and suitable amounts
of healthy fats. Limiting excessive added sugars, highly processed foods, and excess sodium can be useful for
many people, although individual needs differ.
Physical activity supports cardiovascular fitness, muscle function, metabolic health, and overall well-being.

metabolic health, and overall well-being. A
practical activity plan should account for a person's current fitness level, injuries, medical conditions, and
preferences. Gradual progression is generally more sustainable than sudden extreme increases in exercise.
Sleep is also relevant to health. Regular sleep timing, a comfortable sleep environment, and reducing
stimulating activities close to bedtime can support healthy sleep habits.

to bedtime can support healthy sleep habits. Persistent or severe sleep problems
may warrant professional evaluation.
Preventive care can include vaccinations, age- and risk-appropriate screening, dental care, eye care, and
routine medical visits. The correct screening schedule is not identical for everyone.

Page 6

Symptoms are signals rather than diagnoses. The same symptom may have many possible explanations. RAG
answers should therefore avoid converting a general symptom description into a definitive diagnosis.

Examples of possible contexts

A useful RAG response to a symptom question can describe the general possibilities contained in the
knowledge base, identify warning signs, and explain what additional information may matter. It should not
claim certainty about an individual user's condition.

Page 7
5. Diabetes and Metabolic Health
Diabetes is a group of conditions involving elevated blood glucose over time. Different forms of diabetes have
different causes and management considerations. The body may have insufficient insulin production, reduced
response to insulin, or a combination of factors depending on the type and individual circumstances.

on the type and individual circumstances.
Commonly discussed symptoms of elevated blood glucose can include increased thirst, frequent urination,
increased hunger, fatigue, blurred vision, and unexplained changes in body weight. However, some people may
have few or no obvious symptoms, especially early in the disease process.
Diagnosis of diabetes is based on established laboratory criteria rather than symptoms alone.

laboratory criteria rather than symptoms alone. Common tests
include measures of blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), with interpretation depending on the
clinical context and applicable diagnostic standards.
Diabetes management may include nutrition planning, physical activity, glucose monitoring when indicated,
medicines, and regular follow-up. The appropriate treatment depends on diabetes type, glucose patterns, other
health factors, and clinician guidance.

other
health factors, and clinician guidance.
Possible long-term complications can involve blood vessels, nerves, kidneys, eyes, and other organs. Risk
reduction commonly involves maintaining appropriate glucose control and addressing other cardiovascular and
metabolic risk factors.
Hypoglycemia refers to abnormally low blood glucose. Symptoms can include shakiness, sweating, hunger,
weakness, confusion, or changes in behavior.

weakness, confusion, or changes in behavior. Severe hypoglycemia can be an emergency and may require
immediate assistance.

cells.

preceding few months.
Hyperglycemia
A term for elevated blood glucose.

Hyperglycemia
A term for elevated blood glucose.

Lifestyle management
May include nutrition, physical activity, sleep, weight-related goals when appropriate, and
other individualized measures.
Example retrieval question: “What is the difference between hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia?

retriever should surface the glossary or diabetes section even if the question does not use the exact wording
found in the document.

Page 9
6. Cardiovascular Health
The cardiovascular system includes the heart and blood vessels. Cardiovascular health is influenced by factors
such as blood pressure, blood lipids, tobacco exposure, diabetes, physical activity, diet, body composition, age,
family history, and other medical factors.
High blood pressure, also called hypertension, can occur without noticeable symptoms. This is one reason
blood pressure measurement is important.

reason
blood pressure measurement is important. Persistently elevated blood pressure can increase the risk of
cardiovascular and kidney complications.
Cholesterol is a lipid involved in cell membranes and other biological functions. Blood lipid testing may include
measures such as LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. Interpretation depends on overall
cardiovascular risk rather than a single number in isolation.
Chest discomfort can have many causes.

isolation.
Chest discomfort can have many causes. Some forms of chest pressure, especially when accompanied by
shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, fainting, or discomfort spreading to the arm, shoulder, back, neck, or
jaw, can indicate a medical emergency.
A heart-healthy lifestyle may include regular physical activity, a balanced dietary pattern, avoidance of tobacco,
appropriate sleep, and management of blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose when needed.

Page 10
7. Respiratory Health
The respiratory system includes the airways and lungs and is responsible for moving oxygen into the body and
removing carbon dioxide. Respiratory symptoms can result from infections, allergies, asthma, environmental
exposures, chronic lung conditions, cardiovascular conditions, and other causes.
Asthma is a condition characterized by variable airway narrowing and inflammation. Symptoms can include
wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath.

chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Triggers vary and can include allergens,
exercise, respiratory infections, smoke, and environmental irritants.
A respiratory infection may produce cough, sore throat, congestion, fever, fatigue, or other symptoms. The
exact cause cannot always be determined from symptoms alone. Hydration, rest, symptom monitoring, and
appropriate professional advice may be relevant depending on the illness.

advice may be relevant depending on the illness.
Warning signs can include severe breathing difficulty, bluish or gray discoloration of lips or face, severe chest
pain, confusion, inability to stay awake, or rapidly worsening symptoms. These situations require urgent
medical attention.

Page 11
8. Digestive Health
The digestive system processes food and absorbs nutrients. Common digestive complaints include abdominal
discomfort, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, bloating, heartburn, and changes in appetite.
Acid reflux occurs when stomach contents move upward into the esophagus. Symptoms may include heartburn
or a sour taste.

Symptoms may include heartburn
or a sour taste. Symptoms that are frequent, severe, or associated with difficulty swallowing, bleeding,
unexplained weight loss, or significant chest pain should be evaluated by a healthcare professional.
Constipation can involve infrequent bowel movements, hard stools, straining, or a feeling of incomplete
evacuation. Hydration, dietary fiber, physical activity, and medication review can be relevant, but persistent or
severe symptoms need appropriate evaluation.

or
severe symptoms need appropriate evaluation.
Diarrhea can cause fluid and electrolyte loss. Important considerations include duration, severity, ability to drink,
blood in stool, fever, severe abdominal pain, and signs of dehydration.
Digestive symptoms often overlap across conditions. A chatbot should therefore ask or acknowledge context
such as duration, severity, associated symptoms, recent foods, medications, travel, and known conditions when
those details are relevant.

Page 12
9. Women's Health
Women's health includes reproductive health, menstrual health, pregnancy-related care, breast health, bone
health, cardiovascular health, and many other areas. Individual recommendations depend strongly on age,
reproductive status, symptoms, medications, and personal history.
The menstrual cycle varies between individuals and can also change over time.

individuals and can also change over time. Changes in cycle length, flow,
pain, or missed periods can have many possible causes, including stress, changes in weight or activity,
hormonal conditions, pregnancy, medications, and other medical conditions.
Pregnancy can alter which medicines, tests, foods, and activities are appropriate.

tests, foods, and activities are appropriate. A person who may be
pregnant should consult an appropriate healthcare professional before making medication changes or using
treatments that may not be suitable during pregnancy.
Pelvic pain, unusually heavy bleeding, bleeding after menopause, severe pain, fainting, or
pregnancy-associated pain or bleeding can require prompt medical evaluation depending on the
circumstances.

Page 13
10. Mental and Sleep Health
Mental well-being can influence sleep, concentration, appetite, energy, and daily functioning. Stress can
produce physical and emotional symptoms, but persistent or severe symptoms may have multiple causes and
should not automatically be attributed to stress.
Insomnia refers to difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or obtaining restorative sleep despite an opportunity
to sleep.

sleep despite an opportunity
to sleep. Helpful sleep habits can include consistent sleep and wake times, a comfortable sleep environment,
limiting late-day stimulants when appropriate, and using a calming pre-sleep routine.
Persistent low mood, severe anxiety, major changes in functioning, or thoughts of self-harm warrant
professional support. Immediate danger or thoughts of acting on self-harm require urgent local emergency or
crisis assistance.

urgent local emergency or
crisis assistance.
A health chatbot should use supportive, nonjudgmental language and should not present itself as a replacement
for a clinician or crisis professional.

Page 14
11. Medication and Safety Concepts
Medicines can be beneficial but can also cause side effects, interactions, allergic reactions, or problems when
used incorrectly. The correct dose and schedule depend on the specific medicine, formulation, person,
indication, kidney and liver function, other medicines, and other factors.
A chatbot should not invent a dose or tell a person to start, stop, or change a prescription medicine based only
on a general question.

medicine based only
on a general question. It can explain general concepts from a trusted knowledge source and recommend
discussing personal treatment decisions with a pharmacist or clinician.
Medication reconciliation means reviewing all medicines a person uses, including prescriptions,
over-the-counter products, vitamins, supplements, and sometimes topical or inhaled products. This can help
identify duplication, interactions, or confusion about schedules.

interactions, or confusion about schedules.
Allergic reactions to medicines can range from mild rash to severe reactions involving breathing difficulty,
facial or throat swelling, fainting, or other serious symptoms. Severe allergic symptoms require urgent medical
attention.

Page 16
13. Frequently Asked Questions
What is blood pressure?
Blood pressure is the force of circulating blood against blood vessel walls. It is commonly reported using systolic
and diastolic measurements. A single reading does not always represent a person's usual blood pressure.
What is a normal body temperature?
Body temperature varies by person, measurement method, time of day, and other factors.

method, time of day, and other factors. Fever is generally
discussed in relation to an elevated temperature, but the exact interpretation depends on context and the
measurement method.
Why can someone feel tired?
Fatigue has many possible causes, including insufficient sleep, stress, infection, anemia, medication effects,
metabolic conditions, and other health problems. Persistent or unexplained fatigue may warrant evaluation.
What does dehydration mean?

warrant evaluation.
What does dehydration mean?
Dehydration occurs when fluid loss exceeds fluid intake. Thirst, dry mouth, reduced urination, dizziness,
weakness, and dark urine can occur, although symptoms vary.
Does one symptom prove a disease?
No. Symptoms usually have multiple possible causes, and diagnosis generally requires context, history,
examination, and sometimes testing.
What is an allergy?
An allergy is an immune response to a substance that is otherwise harmless to many people.

that is otherwise harmless to many people. Symptoms can
range from mild to severe.
What is inflammation?
Inflammation is a biological response involving immune and tissue processes. It can occur with infection, injury,
autoimmune processes, and other stimuli.
What is a risk factor?
A risk factor is a characteristic, behavior, exposure, or condition associated with a change in the likelihood of
developing a disease. A risk factor does not guarantee that a person will develop the disease.

guarantee that a person will develop the disease.
Why does a RAG chatbot need sources?
Retrieval supplies relevant source material to the language model. This can improve grounding and make it
possible to inspect which passages support an answer, although retrieval alone does not guarantee
correctness.
What should a chatbot do when the answer is not in the document?
It should say that the available knowledge base does not contain enough information and avoid inventing facts.

enough information and avoid inventing facts.
A production system can optionally direct the user to an appropriate professional or verified external source.

14. RAG Test-Question Bank
Use these questions after building your retrieval system. Do not immediately look at the answer section;
instead, inspect which chunks your retriever returns.
1. What is the difference between a symptom and a sign?
2. Why can fatigue have many possible causes?
3. What are some commonly discussed symptoms of elevated blood glucose?
4. What is HbA1c used for?
5. What is the difference between hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia?
6.

between hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia?
6. Why can high blood pressure be difficult to notice?
7. What factors can influence cardiovascular health?
8. What respiratory symptoms can occur with asthma?
9. What warning signs may require urgent attention for breathing problems?
10. What factors can be relevant when evaluating digestive symptoms?
11. Why can menstrual changes have multiple possible causes?
12. Why should medication changes be discussed with a professional?
13.

changes be discussed with a professional?
13. What is medication reconciliation?
14. What warning signs can require urgent medical attention?
15. What should the chatbot do if the document does not contain an answer?
16. Find information about a concept using a synonym rather than the exact term used in the document.
17. Ask a question whose answer requires combining information from two different sections.
18.

information from two different sections.
18. Ask a question that should return a warning/callout rather than a disease explanation.
Advanced retrieval tests: Try “What are signs of low sugar?” instead of “What are symptoms of
hypoglycemia?” Try “high sugar” instead of “hyperglycemia.” Try “breathing problem” instead of “respiratory
symptom.” These paraphrases help you evaluate semantic retrieval.

Chunking exercise: create chunks using at least three strategies and compare the results.

least three strategies and compare the results. Strategy A can use a
fixed character size with overlap. Strategy B can split on paragraphs and then apply a maximum size. Strategy
C can use sentence-aware or recursive splitting. For every strategy, inspect whether important ideas remain
together and whether chunks contain enough context to answer questions.
Embedding exercise: embed every chunk and store the vector with its metadata. Then embed a user query and
retrieve the most similar chunks.

user query and
retrieve the most similar chunks. Record the similarity score, chunk ID, section, and text. This creates a
transparent bridge between the conceptual RAG diagram and your implementation.
Generation exercise: construct a prompt containing the user question and retrieved context. Tell the model to
use only the provided context, avoid unsupported medical claims, and say when the context is insufficient.
Evaluation exercise: measure retrieval separately from generation.

measure retrieval separately from generation. A response can sound fluent while still
being poorly grounded. First ask: “Did the correct evidence appear in the retrieved chunks?” Then ask: “Did
the final answer accurately use that evidence? the final answer accurately use that evidence? ”

Page 19
RAG Learning Cheat Sheet
Ingestion: Source → Load → Parse → Clean → Chunk → Embed → Store
Retrieval: User Query → Embed Query → Search Vector Store → Retrieve Top-K Chunks
Augmentation: Retrieved Context + User Question → Prompt
Generation: Prompt → LLM → Grounded Answer
Key distinction: RAG is an application architecture/pattern. LangChain is a framework that can help
implement parts of that architecture.
This document is deliberately designed for RAG experimentation.

retrieval, prompt construction, and evaluation.
